The first step is to separate the point from the flat. - This will take a skilled butcher 90 seconds to do correctly and a novice maybe 15 minutes... You need to follow the fat-line between the 2 cuts pretty precisely in order to leave a bit of fat on both sides. if you have to err, leave the fat on the point, not the flat. so once the meat is trimmed you're ready to brine it:

Get a cooler, or a 5-gallon bucket with a lid or something which can hold a significant volume of liquid... most people probably measure this but I just grew up with it... heat up the tap water to as hot as it will go and start filling your vessel with warm water. as you fill it, take a big $1 box of cheap salt (NO IODINE - it fucks up the flavor) and start pouring it into the water... stir as you go - don't entirely saturate the solution but try to get as close as you can to making the water/salt mixture achieve a balance where neither can absorb any more of the other... try to fill your vessel about 1/3 of the way to achieve this blend... if you go higher than 1/2 you may overflow when you start adding meat.

before you add the meat add a bunch of ice.disclaimer. while your meat takes its salt bath it's time to think about your flavor profile. I won't go too into detail here because I don't want to share my recipe and we all like different things, but you need a balance of: "sweet, heat, salt and smoke" - My rubs are usually about 1/3 brown sugar. I know that sounds like a lot, but that's what forms the bark and makes it dark and sticky and bbq. NO SALT. all the salt was in the brine. if you did it right the brine has been sucked through the whole cut of meat now and it's perfectly salted.

after the sugar the next big thing needs to be some form of a pepper... sweet or hot from paprika to cayenne but pepper-based. (i like a blend of paprika and ancho as the foundation with a good portion of chipotle and a little dash of cayenne, but whatever you're into - this combo should be about 1/3 of the total reb)... and you need some black-pepper - at least "something" to balance the flavor... on up to however much you're into.

You need 1 herb (you can use more, but you need 1) - I like marjoram. - oregano and thyme are next on the list - but again, eat what you like.

other popular ingredients are: garlic, onion, chili-powder, mustard-seed/ground-mustard, celery seed, cumin, lemon-pepper... there's no limit here. go with what you like.

what most people really key-in-on as the bbq flavor is a little bit of allspice or clove or cinnamon - not much - but enough to bring in that "other" element in.

when it's all mixed up it should be orange-ish since the peppers and brown-sugar make up 2/3 of the mix.

I like to mix a fruit wood and a nut wood.... usually just 1 of each. as a general rule hickory is a stronger nut wood than pecan and cherry is a stronger fruit wood than apple. get the coals going and add them to the smoker... if you have an indirect smoker you're shooting for 250-275-degrees or so (300 won't kill you if it's a shorter spike... try not to get hotter than that. 200 will really slow your cooking) You'll need to check the temp every 20-30min and learn how your own smoker works... add mainly charcoal... like 80/20 charcoal/wood.... volume will change based on outside temp.

pull your meat from the brine and pat it dry. cover it in the rub... don't go "thick" with it, but make sure to rub it into the whole surface of the meat.

ribs/chicken should take about 4 hours. if it's a chicken start breast DOWN and then flip it over after 2 hours. if it's ribs, start with the arch up for the first 2 hours and then flip to arch down.

The point should be done in 5-8 hours since it's closer to the fire... I like to wrap it in foil and move it to the far corner of the smoker to keep going while the flat finished. after the flat has gone from 4-12 hours (closer to 4 at 275, closer to 12 at 200) pull the shriveled fat off this side and flip it over so the actual fat side is up. you're 1/2 way there.
